Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses dramatized scenes—complete with sharp, realistic dialogue and specific actions (like walking to town, changing the lightbulb, and visiting the hospital)—to reveal the complex, affectionate, and slightly stubborn dynamic between the mother and the narrator in real time. At the same time, the writer weaves in concise passages of summary and exposition to provide necessary background (such as memories of the late father and childhood anecdotes) and to bridge gaps in time (such as compressing the three ordinary weeks between the June visit and the July heatstroke). This balance keeps the pacing smooth while ensuring the emotional beats of the story feel vivid and earned.
